en: Oṃ, homage to the All-Knowing One,
to the Victor, the Sun among Sages, whose self is the supreme light.

Salutation to the Unmeasured within the night, and to the Maker of Day within the day. [1.1] The purpose of this treatise is that one may personally engage in the composition of poetry and acquire proficiency in the works of others. In this regard, Piṅgala is the source for this *Chandoviciti* (metrics), while Jayadeva is the source for the aphorisms (*sūtra*) and their illustrative examples (*udāharaṇa*). Nevertheless, this work surpasses that [of Piṅgala] by eight qualities. To wit: (1) it contains no abbreviation regarding the *prastāra* (metrical expansion) and other such matters; (2) there is no composition in verse (*śloka-bandha*) concerning the heavy (*guru*), light (*laghu*), and other prosodic elements; (3) for the most part, there is no lack of clarity; and (4) in demonstrating practical application, there is no creation of anything unprecedented.

(5) Even though it is easy to distinguish between the designations of *yati* (caesura) and *saṃjñā* (name), it is not understood [as such]. For example: "In the *Rju* [meter], there are *mayūrasāriṇī*, then *rgau*; in the *Vasujaladhivirāma* [meter], there are *nau* and *puṭā myau*. (6) Furthermore, for *jāti* and the others, [the distinction] from *capuṭa* is easy for those who have studied previously; thus, there is no sequential order [of names] joined together. (7) And in cases such as "The *vaitālīya* has *rlganaidhanāḥ*" [Jayadeva 4.15], the reading is not easy. (8) Since both *yati* and *gaṇa* have unequal divisions, the *gaṇas* do not end with a *yati*.

In this [work], these eight qualities are present: [it is composed of] sūtras, examples, and so forth. Therefore, it is superior even to that [other work]. And there is a verse on this point: "Conciseness, metrical form, clarity, sūtras, examples, composition, non-confusion, sequence, recitation, and mastery of pauses—these are the qualities."
A *padya* consists of four lines (*catuṣpadī*), and it is of two kinds according to the distinction between *vṛtta* and *jāti*:
*vṛtta* is measured by the number of syllables, while *jāti* is measured by the number of morae (*mātrā*). [1.2]

A *padya* consists of four quarters (*catuṣpadī*). That which has four quarters is called *catuṣpadī*. Alternatively, the word *pada* may signify a quarter-part; thus, the collective aggregate of four quarters is *catuṣpadī*, and that is termed a *padya*. Furthermore, that *padya* is of two kinds, distinguished by *vṛtta* and *jāti*. Thus, that *padya* is twofold according to this division: *vṛtta* and *jāti*. *Vṛtta* is measured by the number of syllables (*akṣara*). "Number" (*saṃkhyā*) means counting; that which has its count determined by syllables is *vṛtta*.
The meter is defined by its number of morae. That is called a "meter" (jāti) which is numbered by means of morae.

A short vowel is light; the letter *l* is also light. At the ends of metrical feet, a long vowel (*g*) is generally heavy; so too is a curved consonant (*vakra*), as well as a preceding consonant that lacks a following vowel, and long and protracted vowels. [1.3]

That phoneme which is articulated clearly even by itself is called a vowel (*svara*). Briefly, it is of three types: short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), and protracted (*pluta*). Among these, the short vowel consists of one *mātrā*. It is fivefold: *a*, *i*, *u*, *ṛ*, and *ḷ*. The long vowel consists of two *mātrās*. It is eightfold: *ā*, *ī*, *ṝ*, *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au*. The protracted vowel consists of three *mātrās*. It is ninefold; just as the eight long vowels are written, so too are the eight protracted vowels, distinguished only by the addition of the numeral three. The ninth is the sound *ḷ* with the numeral three.

Thus, there are twenty-two vowels. Those phonemes which do not clearly sound out by themselves are the consonants (*vyañjana*), numbering thirty-seven: thirty-three beginning with *ka* and ending with *ha*, plus the four—*anusvāra*, *visarjanīya*, *jihvāmūlīya*, and *upadhmānīya*. Thus, there are fifty-nine phonemes (*varṇa*) in this treatise. In the calculation of syllables (*akṣara*), however, only the vowels are counted, not the consonants. And on this point, there is a verse: The vowels are the syllables; the consonants are not. The consonants are for the purpose of manifesting the vowels. Just as a cart cannot move by its two wheels alone, So too, the consonants cannot produce a syllable without the vowels.

There are thirty-seven consonants (*vyañjana*) and twenty-two vowels (*svara*) here; these fifty-nine phonemes (*varṇa*) constitute the syllable (*akṣara*), which is to be counted by its vowels. A short vowel is light (*laghu*); it is straight (*ṛju*). A short vowel is light; it is called *la* by name, and it is straight by its placement-line. [The meter is] well-constructed: ◡ ◡ ◡ ◡ ◡ ◡. At the ends of quarters (*pādānta*), a long vowel (*guru*) is frequent; it is curved (*vakra*). A short vowel—at the ends of quarters—is frequently [light].

A syllable becomes heavy (*guru*) by its name; and it is also "crooked" (*vakra*) by virtue of the line of placement (*nyāsarekhā*). Why say "frequently"? So that it does not apply in cases such as *samānī* and others. It should apply elsewhere at the end of even quarters, as in *indravajrā* and other meters, and at the end of odd quarters. [The rule continues: A short vowel preceding a consonant that is itself devoid of a vowel is also heavy and "crooked. For example: *mṛtyuḥ kiṃ kḷptaḥ*— — — — —. Long and protracted vowels are likewise [heavy].

Every long vowel (*dīrgha*) and protracted vowel (*pluta*) is heavy (*guru*), as is a syllable with a *krama* (vowel doubling). Feminine endings (*nārī*), the dual number (*nṛtū*), and the case endings of the two divine classes (*daiva*) [are heavy]. Even a protracted vowel (*pluta*) is heavy. For example: *indro3 agnī3*; *kḷ3ptaśikhaḥ*.

The first three [syllables] are desired as heavy (guru), the second as light (laghu), the third as heavy, and all [four] as heavy; likewise, the first as light, the second as light, the third as light, and all [four] as light are desired. [1.4]

A group of three syllables with a long (heavy) syllable at the beginning is desired as *bha*. A "group of three" (*trika*) consists of three syllables. That group of three which has a long syllable at the beginning is desired to be designated by the name *bha*—◡ ◡ ◡. It has a long syllable at the beginning; that which has a long syllable at the very beginning is "beginning-long" (*ādiguru*). This should be understood in the same way for the subsequent [designations] as well. A group of three syllables with a long syllable in the middle is desired as *ja*. That which is desired as *ja* is designated by the name *ja*—◡ ◡ ◡. A group of three syllables with a long syllable at the end is desired as *sa*. That group of three which is desired as *sa* is designated by the name *sa*—◡ ◡ ◡.

*m* is entirely heavy; that group of three which is entirely heavy is designated as *ma*. *y* begins with a light [syllable]; that group of three which begins with a light syllable is designated as *ya*. *r* has a light syllable in the middle; that group of three which has a light syllable in the middle is designated as *ra*. *t* has a light syllable at the end; that group of three which has a light syllable at the end is designated as *ta*. *n* is entirely light.

That group of three syllables which consists entirely of short (laghu) syllables is designated as *na*. These eight: those three-syllable groups (*gaṇas*) are eight in number; they are *bha*, *ja*, *sa*, *ma*, *ya*, *ra*, *ta*, and *na*. Wherever these letters are recited, one should remember that the mnemonic rules (*saṃjñā-sūtras*) begin with those respective letters: *bha* has a long syllable at the beginning; *ja* has a long syllable in the middle; *sa* has a long syllable at the end; *ma* has long syllables throughout; *ya* has a short syllable at the beginning; *ra* has a short syllable in the middle; *ta* has a short syllable at the end; and *na* has short syllables throughout.
The meters are known through groups of six, beginning with one foot and increasing by one for each subsequent meter:
Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Paṅkti, and likewise Triṣṭubh. [1.5]

They know the *chandāṃsi* (Vedic meters) by means of groups of six, with feet increasing one by one, because the names of the meters depend upon their metrical feet (*vṛtta*). Beginning with feet of six syllables, they know the meters through feet that increase by one syllable thereafter: *gāyatrī*, *uṣṇih*, *anuṣṭubh*, *bṛhatī*, *paṅkti*, and likewise *triṣṭubh*. The science of prosody (*chandoviciti*) follows a systematic sequence; therefore, the names of the meters are connected according to this order. With feet of six syllables, it is *gāyatrī*.
With seven syllables it is the *uṣṇih*; with eight syllables, the *anuṣṭubh*; with nine syllables, the *bṛhatī*; with ten syllables, the *paṅkti*; and with eleven syllables, the *triṣṭubh*.
The Jagatīśakvarī, the Aṣṭidhṛti, the Pṛthak, the Kevalā, the Atiparā, the Śuddhā, the Prāvi, the Samabhyutparā, and the Kṛti—these are the six types consisting of eight and seven [syllables]. [1.6]

The *jagatī*, *śakvarī*, *aṣṭi*, and *dhṛti* are each individually and exclusively *atiparā*. The word "individually" (*pṛthak*) has the sense of "each one. Those meters which follow immediately after the *triṣṭubh* are called by the names *jagatī* and so forth; each of them is individually and exclusively *atiparā*. With twelve syllables per foot, it is *jagatī*; with thirteen syllables per foot, *atijagatī*; with fourteen syllables, *śakvarī*; with fifteen syllables, *atiśakvarī*; and with sixteen syllables, *aṣṭi*.

With seventeen syllables [per quarter] it is *atyaṣṭi*; with eighteen syllables, *dhṛti*; with nineteen syllables, *atidhṛti*. Why are these mentioned separately? So that the sequence of names—*jagatī*, *śakvarī*, *aṣṭi*, *dhṛti*, and *atijagatī*, *atiśakvarī*, *atyaṣṭi*, *atidhṛti*—does not occur. *Kṛti* is preceded by *pra*, *vi*, *sam*, *abhi*, *ud*, and *para*. Beyond this, the meter is simply *kṛti*; it is also designated by name when preceded by *pra* and the others. With twenty-syllable quarters, it is *kṛti*.

With twenty-one syllables is *prakṛti*; with twenty-two syllables is *ākṛti*; with twenty-three syllables is *vikṛti*; with twenty-four syllables is *saṃkṛti*; with twenty-five syllables is *abhikṛti*; with twenty-six syllables is *utkṛti*. Thus are the six, the eight, and the horses (*hayas*). Those meters which have been declared by these sūtras are, in their respective order, the six, the eight, and the horses; the horses being seven.

For objects whose numbers are well-known indicate a specific count. For example: one form; two twins; three fires; four Vedas and oceans; five arrows, senses, and objects; six seasons and tastes; seven worlds, horses, and sages; eight Vasus, limbs, and Madana; nine apertures and planets; ten directions; eleven Rudras; twelve suns; thirteen worlds; fourteen Manus.

Note: Regarding the enumeration of *bhūta*s, it is said that meter (*vṛtta*) is of three kinds: even (*sama*), half-even (*ardhasama*), and uneven (*viṣama*). These are, respectively, the *tanumadhyā* group, the *upacitraka* group, and the *vaktra* group. [1.7]

They declare that *vṛtta* (meter) is of three kinds: even (*sama*), half-even (*ardhasama*), and uneven (*viṣama*). These correspond respectively to the *tanumadhyā* class and so forth, the *upacitrā* class and so forth, and the *vaktra* class and so forth. Indeed, they say that *vṛtta* is of exactly three types: even, half-even, and uneven; and these, in their respective order, are the *tanumadhyā* class and so forth, the *upacitrā* class and so forth, and the *vaktra* class and so forth.
The pause occurs at the end of the quarters with the desired number of syllables;
that which possesses it has *uti* as its beginning, and *g-volkaḥ* follows in each quarter. [1.8]

The pause (*yati*) is the resting place desired [by the poet]. "Resting place," "staying," "rest," and "pause" are synonyms. That pause which occurs at desired syllables is called *yati*; it applies to both *vṛtta* (metrical) and *jāti* (prosodic) compositions. [Example: *gaṇḍasvedāpanayanarujāklāntakarṇotpalānām | praṇamacchaśāṅkamaulidviguṇīkṛtacaraṇanakhakiraṇāḥ ||* Why say "desired"? It is so that it does not occur at undesired places. [Example: *eṣa kṣitipo vikhyātasphuṭakīrtir yasya dhvajinī ketūdastaghanaughā ||* [The pause occurs] at the end of the *caraṇas* (quarters).

A pause (*yati*) occurs at the end of the feet [of a verse]. That which possesses it begins with *u* and so forth. The word "end" (*anta*) is understood to carry over. When the syllable *u* is present, the eightfold class of ganas beginning with *bha* should be known as possessing a pause at the end. *g vaḥ*: A heavy (*guru*) syllable possessing a pause should be known by the name *va*. *l kaḥ*: A light (*laghu*) syllable possessing a pause has the name *ka*. These three sūtras are for the purpose of defining the regularity of the pause. For even in common worldly usage, having set aside uneven pauses, one practices a regular pause... the pause... is practiced.
This heading applies to even meters (samavṛtta) for each quarter-verse (pāda).

[2.1] If *tyau*—that is, if the syllables *ta* and *ya* occur at the beginning of each quarter-verse (*pāda*)—then the meter named *tanumadhyā* arises. In this treatise, the aphorism (*sūtra*) itself serves as the example; therefore, the metrical expansion (*prastāra*) must be performed using the very letters of the aphorism: ◡ ◡ — —. The phrase "if *tyau*" indicates the body of the definition. The pause (*yati*) occurs at the ends of the quarters. The term "at each quarter" (*pratipādam*) establishes the connection between these two [syllables] and the quarters. *Tanumadhyā* is the technical name (*saṃjñā*). This should be understood in the same way for what follows hereafter.

May those two feet, rich with the characteristics just described and possessing various variations,
have both their metrical pauses and their elaborate expansions worthy of being heard.
Those are known as *upajātis* by the masters of tradition.

[2.18] Those two feet, rich with the characteristics described immediately above, may consist of various combinations; those whose both feet possess an elaborate and melodious caesura are known as *upajātis* by the masters of tradition. Those two feet endowed with the characteristics of *indravajrā* and *upendravajrā* mentioned just prior—when both of them possess an elaborate and melodious caesura—they are known as *upajātis* by the lords of tradition.

How can both feet come to possess various combinations according to their respective application, through the occurrence [of syllables] in one, two, or three positions, resulting in fourteen modes? There is a distinction in the initial syllables, and there are four feet. Therefore, having performed the *prastāra* (metrical expansion) as for a four-syllable meter, it should be demonstrated: at the top is *Indravajrā*, at the bottom is *Upendravajrā*, and in between are the fourteen *Upajāti*s.

How are these "analytical methods"? Because by means of them, specific characteristics that are otherwise unknown are easily understood. Furthermore, confidence arises through the superior knowledge of the authors of the treatises, just as the movements of Rāhu and other celestial bodies are understood by an astrologer skilled in calculation.
